Goals of an AI-First and Agentic Development Process

 

To accelerate the rate at which we can deliver functional and quality code, we want to employ an approach to code generation that is:

  • AI-First
  • and Agentic

 

In addition, the goal of an AI-First SDLC is to incorporate AI into every facet of the software development process:

 

 

Why Agentic?

 

  • Multi-step coding tasks become more seamless via specifications given to the agent
  • Greater control over the structure and quality of the code via agent instructions
  • Can incorporate all aspects of the cycle into a change:  Tests, code, local execution, review
  • Naturally enhances documentation of requirements


 

To effectively accomplish this, we need a process that is optimized for agents:

  1. The best tools AI models for interacting with agents
  2. Agents should clearly understand what to solve for each feature regardless of the technical implementation
  3. Agents must know how to go about solving it, what rules apply, and how it should organize the work
  4. Generated code must be secure, maintainable, performant and follow standards
  5. We must have a way to measure, observe and validate AI-generated code.
     


Approved Agent Tools and Models

There are two primary tools available today for AI-powered development at Paycor:

  1. GitHub Copilot – Default tool accessible to all engineers

  2. Claude Code – Currently being piloted by one team.  The organization is exploring the option to make available by request for users with more complex requirements

     

For an agentic approach with GitHub Copilot, make sure your chat mode is set to Agent:

 

 

 

Model selection:  

 

In GitHub Copilot, use Claude Sonnet 4.5 for primary, larger coding tasks as it has been proven to produce higher quality code.  Use GPT-4.1 or GPT-5 mini for smaller, less impactful changes.

Only models associated with your Paycor GitHub account may be selected.  Do not use a personal account with GitHub Copilot.

In Claude Code, recommendation is to use Opus 4.1 for more complex tasks (higher cost) and use Sonnet 4/4.5 for smaller, more typical development tasks.

Step 1: Optimizing your environment for Copilot

An optimal environment for agentic development should include the following:

 

  1. Base instruction files to guide the agent for each activity.  Contains general rules about the workspace/codebase layout and how to approach the code

  2. Coding, architectural and pattern guidelines within additional instruction files

  3. Installation of a framework for creating and managing specification documents for the agent

  4. Product and feature specifications that serve as memory for the design of the application

  5. Task history of what the agent is to complete and has completed

Workspace Options

 

Copilot can be configured to work within

  1. An individual repository

  2. Within a workspace that references multiple repositories (VS Code).

 

Why would I want to configure at a workspace level?  If you are performing work that spans multiple repositories such as frontend/backend, integration of a feature across apps, etc. there can be value in creating specifications and instructions that span multiple repositories.  The benefit of sharing context this way is the agent can get a more complete picture of all the work to be performed and can create a more accurate and comprehensive plan.

 

See this guidance for setting up the agent to work within a VS Code workspace:  Working-with-Copilot-+-Agent-OS-in-a-multi-repository-workspace-(VS-Code-Only)-.aspx

 

 

Installing the Paycor AI SDLC Toolkit

 

Follow the instructions here to bootstrap your codebase with the core spec-driven development files: 

 

NOTE:  The below commands are using the Paycor private NPM repository.  If you need to configure your environment to connect to this, follow the steps here:  Connect to Feed - Azure Artifacts

 

Method 1: NPX (Recommended)

Use NPX to run the installer without installing it globally:

 
npx @paycor/ai-sdlc-toolkit

Method 2: Global Installation

Install globally for repeated use:

 
npm install -g @paycor/ai-sdlc-toolkit
create-ai-sdlc

 

 

Creating Instruction Files

 

Every codebase should contain a base set of instructions to inform the coding agent of the project layout and enforce patterns/rules in the code. Instruction files apply to all code changes made in the repository when using Agent mode and are not specific to any feature.

You can create both base instructions that get added to every request made to Copilot and also custom instruction files that conditionally apply based on the type of code being edited.

 

  • VS Code

    Getting baseline instructions created:  Click Chat Window -> Click Settings at the top -> Generate Agent Instructions

  • Visual Studio:  Adding repository custom instructions for GitHub Copilot - GitHub Docs

     

    Comprehensive Instructions

Enhancing the instructions further

Review and ask the agent to refine the instructions as needed to cover basic aspects of code development

  • Project organization expectations

  • Clean code principles

  • Coding style

  • Security rules

  • Data access layer rules

  • Language features

  • Exception handling rules

  • Performance best practices

 

Additional Custom Instruction Files

 

VS Code:  

Additional custom instructions can be added to the .github/instructions directory in your codebase, named with the pattern ******.instructions.md.  These can be used to apply additional rules conditionally based on the type of code being modified.  

Example custom instructions

 

Visual Studio:

VS only supports a single instructions file.  You can copy/paste the contents of your custom instructions into the main copilot-instructions.md file.

Step 2: Using a Spec-Driven Development Flow and Context Engineering

The Specification-Driven Agentic Flow

 

By first creating specifications for the agent to follow and storing them as physical files in your codebase, a spec-driven flow enables agents to work iteratively with less hand-holding:

  1.  Create product spec:  Tell the agent how your codebase is organized (product/codebase specs)

  2.  Create feature spec:  Give a clear description of each feature / business process to build (feature specification)

  3.  Create technical spec:  Have the agent provide a plan for how to technically implement it (technical specification)

  4.  Have the agent provide a task list to work from in small increments (it is optimized for small, iterative tasks)

  5.  Execute the tasks and review along the way

 

Frameworks

  • Agent OS (Buildermethods) - Ready for Use

  • Spec-Kit (GitHub) - Currently Under Evaluation

  • Others (Analysis Pending)

 

 

Using Agent-OS

 

Agent OS takes advantage of GitHub’s custom instructions feature, which allows multiple instruction files to be placed under the .github/instructions directory.

 

  • Once you've installed the necessary files from the toolkit described earlier, you can use the following prompts to get started.

plan-product    - Initiate Agent OS in a new product's codebase

analyze-product - Initiate Agent OS in an existing product's codebase

create-spec     - Initiate a new feature

execute-tasks - Execute tasks

 

  • How to run the commands:

    • VS Code:  In the agent chat, type a slash (/) followed by the command and select the prompt to use

    • Visual Studio:  Type #prompt: followed by the command and then select the prompt to use

 

 

Executing the Spec-Driven Workflow:

 

  1. /analyze-product:  Generate Additional Codebase information (Product Specs)

 

  • For New Codebases:  Leverage the /plan-product prompt (Agent OS) to create an initial product specification

  • For Existing Codebases:  Leverage the /analyze-product prompt (Agent OS) to scan the codebase and generate a detailed specification that describes your codebase.

    • VS Code:  type /analyze-product and select the prompt from the context menu.  Once selected, submit the prompt in the chat.

      • Note:  If you don't see the context menu show up like below or if you don't see /analyze-product highlighted like below, check to make sure you the Agent OS prompt files exist under .github/prompts

         

         

    • Visual Studio:  type #prompt: and then select analyze-product.prompt.md

  • It will then go through a process to generate a set of files within your .agent-os directory at the root of your repository.

  • Review the files and if needed ask Copilot to refine the documents and summarize key modules, dependencies, and principles.

  • This gives the agent a clear map of your code’s organization and conventions

  • Claude Code:  Use Agent OS or ask it to initialize your repository with a CLAUDE.md file

 

2. /create-spec:  Create Feature + Technical Specifications

 

  • Using the /create-spec command (Agent OS) or Plan mode (Claude Code), ask the agent to create a detailed specification document for each new feature.

    • VS Code:

      • Type /create-spec followed by a description of the feature you want to create.  Add detailed information about the purpose of the feature, business logic and high-level implementation details.

    • Visual Studio:

      • Type #prompt: and then select created-spec.prompt.md.  Then type a description of the feature you want to create.  Add detailed information about the purpose of the feature, business logic and high-level implementation details.

            •  
  • The agent should then generate a set of markdown files in your .agent-os/specs directory with detailed requirements

  • Feature spec documents are focused on just the problem to be solved and are different from technical implementation specs.

  • Include information about key aspects such as user interaction, security requirements, key endpoints to be leveraged, tech stack requirements, how to break down the code modules, etc.

  • Leverage details from PBIs to enhance the spec creation process.

  • Ask AI to optimize your initial prompt for use with the coding agent.

 

  • Review each specification document and ask the agent for modifications where needed.  Iterate on the document to ensure it aligns with the goal and that the solution is not overly complex.

  • A few things to look for:

    • Redundant code – does the plan create redundant functionality?
    • Reusability – is the plan creating shared services that are too specific?
    • Is the solution overly complex?  Is there a simpler way to approach the problem?


 

3. Create the task list - a granular set of sequential tasks the agent should follow to build the feature

 

  • With the spec open in your editor, ask the agent to create a task breakdown for executing the plan.  Review the plan prior to any code generation.

  • The agent should then create a detailed breakdown of tasks for it to follow within a tasks.md file

  • A granular set of tasks will allow the agent to efficiently deliver increments that require less context.  It also allows for breakpoints for you to review the code for issues before it gets too far along.

  • Ensure the plan follows key development principles:

    • Individual tasks should be limited in scope and avoid broad changes at once

    • Creation of tests is part of the plan

    • Security logic is being considered

    • There are clear breakpoints in the task list where the feature could be partially tested


 Use history effectively

 

  • Track what the agent does by having it record progress in the task list.  Have it clearly note any issues along the way and don’t let it skip too many steps.  It can be less rework to have it iteratively solve a step than skip it.

  • Manage your conversations effectively.  Don’t always start multiple new features in a single conversation flow.  It is often better to start fresh chats for new features.

  • Also make sure to prompt effectively based on the history.  A new chat will not have all the context related to what you were just asking the agent to do previously.

  • Detailed Context Engineering guidance:  Context Engineering.loop

 

 

4. /execute-tasks:  Execute the Tasks using the framework

  • VS Code

    • Type /execute-tasks in the chat to have the agent begin execution

  • Visual Studio

    • Type #prompt and then select execute-tasks.prompt.md

  • The agent will begin executing the coding tasks and should periodically ask for input

  • Review progress along the way and validate often (does it compile after each step, does it render, do tests pass, etc.)

Tagging AI Generated Code

See AI Attribution

 

 

Drive quality with constant review and feedback

  • Ask the agent to check for errors often before continuing
  • Review all new libraries added by the agent during code generation.  Ensure the agent asks for human confirmation before running any package install command.  Allowing the agent to add new libraries shouldn’t be a frequent activity.
  • Always validate packages the agent adds are free from restrictive licensing and that versions are not outdated.  (link to acceptable licenses TBD)
  • Ensure thorough code reviews to capture mistakes or security issues
  • Don’t let the agent do too much work at once
  • Commit often to your local branch to limit the scope of reverts.  The agent may sometimes need to restore a file from your git history.
  • Coding agents tend to generate verbose and sometimes overly complex code.  Review frequently and ask it to refactor along the way where needed.
  • Continuously update the project instruction/context files to document new features/patterns.
  • Stop the agent early if standards aren’t being followed and ask it to revise the plan
  • Ask the agent to generate code comments in areas of complexity

 

Additional Guidelines

  • Never include customer data, PII or secrets/credentials in prompts
  • Take extra care with agent-generated code that affects IaaC/resource provisioning, critical security code or logic dealing with PII
  • Ensure there is proper code coverage and automated testing of AI-generated code
  • Engineers are ultimately responsible for code they accept from agents.  All agent-created or modified content must follow the same code review, testing, and security policies as human-written code.
  • Complex feature changes should still go through normal design and architectural review.  Agent plans and code are an input, not a replacement.
